title: Bonds, T-Bills and Government Securities
objectives: Describe bond mechanics: face value, coupon, maturity and the issuer/holder relationship
Price discount instruments such as T-bills from their quoted discount rate
Price a coupon bond as the NPV of its cash flows and state the price-yield relationship
Read market conventions: 32nd quotes, ACT/360 day counts and clean vs dirty prices
motivation: Equity gets the headlines; debt gets the money. Bonds are the instrument on which every interest-rate model, yield curve and most collateralised finance is built, and their pricing is a direct application of the NPV machinery from the fundamentals module. This lesson covers the vanilla pieces - bills, notes and bonds - so later lessons can price swaps and futures on top of them.

blocks.md: A bond is a loan you can trade. The **issuer** borrows a stated **face value** (par, typically \$1,000 per bond) and promises two things: periodic **coupon** payments (a percentage of face) and return of face at **maturity**. The holder is the lender; unlike equity, the holder has no ownership and no vote - but a *contractual* claim that ranks ahead of shareholders if the issuer fails. Government securities are the cleanest examples: **T-bills** mature in one year or less, **notes** in 2-10 years, **bonds** beyond that.

A T-bill pays no coupon: it is issued at a **discount** to face and matures at face, the difference being the interest. Bills are quoted with a **discount rate** on an actual/360 day-count, and the price follows immediately:

blocks.caption: Discount-basis pricing: $d$ is the quoted discount rate, days is actual days to maturity.

blocks.title: A 91-day bill with face \$10,000 quoted at a 4.25% discount rate
items: Holding-period return if held to maturity: $107.43 / 9{,}892.57 = 1.086\%$ over 91 days.
Note the subtlety: the discount rate is quoted on *face*, but your return is earned on the *smaller price you pay* - so the true yield is slightly higher than the quoted rate.

blocks.text: Coupon bonds: price = NPV of cash flows

blocks.md: A coupon bond's fair price is the present value of every coupon plus the principal, discounted at the market **yield to maturity (YTM)** - the single rate that equates price and discounted cash flows. For a bond paying an annual coupon $C$, face $F$, maturity $n$ years, at yield $y$:

blocks.caption: Each cash flow gets its own discount factor; the sum is the price.

blocks.md: Governments issue bonds for the same reason corporations do: to spend before taxing, and to term out funding so it does not all come due at once. For a quant, the government curve is not just another asset class — it is the **discounting backbone** of every other valuation on the desk. Equity futures, swaps, options, repo trades: all of them reference a curve that starts here. That is why T-bill and bond mechanics deserve first-class attention rather than a passing nod.

blocks.title: T-bill arithmetic, worked: 90-day bill at 98
items: A T-bill pays no coupons: you pay the price today, receive face (100) at maturity. Quoted here at 98 per 100 face with 90 days remaining.

**Discount yield** (the legacy money-market convention): $(100 - 98)/100 \times 360/90 = 0.02 \times 4 = 8.00\%$. Note the two anachronisms the convention carries: the gain is measured against *face* (not your cost), and the year is 360 days.

**Bond-equivalent yield** (the honest comparison): $(100 - 98)/98 \times 365/90 = 0.020408 \times 4.0556 = 8.277\%$. Measured against the price you actually paid, with the calendar year you actually live in.

The 27.7 basis-point gap is pure convention, not extra money. When someone quotes money-market instruments against bond yields, this is the conversion being (or not being) done — desks have lost real basis points comparing 8.00 to 8.10 across incompatible conventions.

blocks.md: The clean/dirty distinction earns its keep the first time you settle a trade. Between coupon dates, the seller has accrued interest they are owed but will not receive — the next coupon goes entirely to the buyer. So the invoice price is the quoted *clean* price plus *accrued* interest, computed pro-rata on the coupon period. Charts plot clean prices (so the price does not sawtooth down every coupon date); invoices use dirty. Confusing the two is a classic settlement-desk error, and the reconciliation report will find you.

blocks.title: Why the discount curve starts here
blocks.md: A T-bill is the closest thing to a riskless zero-coupon instrument that exists, so its price *is* a discount factor: paying 98 today for 100 in 90 days means $D(0, 0.25) = 0.98$ — no model required. Every curve-fitting method you will meet later is a way of interpolating and smoothing these primitive discount factors into a continuous, arbitrage-free function. The instruments are the raw data; the curve is engineering.

blocks.title: A 2-year, 4% annual-coupon bond (face \$1,000) at a 5% yield
items: Cash flows: \$40 in year 1, \$1,040 in year 2 (coupon + face).
Price $= 38.095238 + 943.310658 = \textbf{\$981.41}$ - below par, because the 5% yield exceeds the 4% coupon.

blocks.title: The price-yield relationship
blocks.md: Price and yield move inversely: a bond's cash flows are fixed, so a higher required return can only be delivered by a lower price. The relationship is convex - prices rise more for a fall in yield than they fall for an equal rise. Duration (a later lesson) measures the slope; the convexity above it is why fixed-income desks smile at both big moves.

blocks.caption: A hypothetical government yield curve (clearly illustrative numbers): short rates above medium, a dip near 5 years, a rise at the long end. Each point prices a bill, note or bond of that maturity - discount every cash flow at its own point, not one flat rate.

blocks.text: Conventions you must not get wrong

items: **Quoting in 32nds**: US Treasury notes and bonds quote as percentages of face in 32nds - "99-16" means $99\tfrac{16}{32} = 99.50$ per \$100 of face, so \$995,000 per \$1m face.
**Day counts**: bills use actual/360 (as above); Treasuries accrue coupon interest on actual/actual; corporate bonds traditionally use 30/360.

**Clean vs dirty price**: quoted (clean) prices exclude accrued interest; you pay the dirty price = clean + accrued coupon since the last payment date, so the seller does not lose the coupon they earned.
**Secondary market reality**: government securities trade predominantly OTC between dealers, not on an exchange book - the plumbing lesson applies.

blocks.md: One habit to carry forward: the *yield curve* is the market's schedule of discount rates by maturity, and every instrument in later lessons - swaps, futures, repo - will be priced against it. This lesson's single-bond arithmetic is the base case: fixed cash flows, one yield, NPV. Everything else is bookkeeping around that core.

guidedExercise.prompt: Price a 2-year bond with a 4% annual coupon and \$1,000 face at a 5% yield: compute each discount factor, discount each cash flow, sum them, and state whether the bond trades at a premium or discount and why.
hints: The final cash flow includes the \$1,000 face plus the last coupon.
guidedExercise.solution: Year 1: $40 \times 0.952381 = 38.095238$. Year 2: $1{,}040 \times 0.907029 = 943.310658$. Price $= \textbf{\$981.41}$. It trades at a **discount** (below \$1,000 par) because the 5% market yield exceeds the 4% coupon - the bond must cheapen until it offers the market's required 5% total return.

independentExercise.prompt: A 182-day T-bill with \$10,000 face is quoted at a 4.8% discount rate (actual/360). (a) Compute its price. (b) Compute the holding-period return to maturity in percent. (c) Approximate the annualised return by multiplying the holding-period return by $365/182$.
independentExercise.solution: (a) Discount $= 10{,}000 \times 0.048 \times 182/360 = 242.67$, so price $= \textbf{$9{,}757.33}$. (b) HPR $= 242.67 / 9{,}757.33 = \textbf{2.487\%}$ over 182 days. (c) Annualised $\approx 0.02487 \times 2.0055 = \textbf{4.99\%}$ - higher than the 4.8% quoted discount rate because the return is earned on the purchase price, not on face.

commonMistakes: Annualising a bill's return on face instead of on the (lower) purchase price - the quoted discount rate understates the true yield.
Assuming price and yield move together: they move inversely, and the curve is convex.
Reading "99-16" as \$99.16 instead of \$99.50 per \$100 face (16/32).
Comparing a clean quote to your settlement cash: the invoice (dirty) price adds accrued interest since the last coupon date.
realWorldApplication: Governments fund deficits by auctioning bills, notes and bonds; banks fund themselves partly in bill markets; central banks implement policy by transacting in exactly these securities - they are the risk-free backbone of the whole rate complex.
quantFinanceApplication: Curve construction from bill and bond prices, discount-factor interpolation and clean/dirty price bookkeeping are the daily bread of fixed-income quant developers; every swap and futures model in later lessons consumes their output.
summary: A bond is a tradable loan: face value repaid at maturity plus coupons; holders rank ahead of shareholders in default.
T-bills are discount instruments: 91 days at a 4.25% discount rate on \$10,000 face prices at \$9,892.57 and earns 1.086% to maturity.
Coupon bond price = NPV of coupons + face at the YTM: the 2-year 4% bond is worth \$981.41 at a 5% yield, \$1,019.13 at 3% - price and yield move inversely, convexly.
Conventions: Treasuries quote in 32nds (99-16 = 99.50), bills use actual/360, and invoices add accrued interest to the clean quote.

quiz.prompt: A 91-day T-bill with \$10,000 face is quoted at a 4.0% discount rate (actual/360). What is its price, to the nearest cent?
A bond's market yield rises above its coupon rate. What happens to its price?
quiz.explanation: Fixed cash flows discounted at a higher rate give a lower price - below par. Par occurs only when yield equals the coupon; yield below coupon gives a premium.

quiz.prompt: A 1-year bond with a 6% annual coupon on \$1,000 face trades at a 7% yield. What is its price, to the nearest cent?
quiz.explanation: Single cash flow: $(60 + 1{,}000)/1.07 = 1{,}060/1.07 = \$990.65$ - a discount, since yield exceeds coupon.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about government securities conventions are correct?
options: Treasury notes and bonds quote in 32nds of a percent of face
T-bills are discount instruments quoted on a discount-rate basis
The clean price already includes accrued interest
quiz.explanation: Bills pay no coupons - they are discount instruments. Notes/bonds quote in 32nds (99-16 = 99.50). The *dirty* price includes accrued interest; the clean price excludes it.

Explain yield to maturity in one sentence and state why a bond's price and its YTM must move in opposite directions.
quiz.modelAnswer: YTM is the single discount rate that equates a bond's price to the present value of its cash flows (its IRR); since the cash flows are fixed, the only way to deliver a higher required return is a lower purchase price, so price and yield move inversely.
quiz.explanation: YTM is the bond's IRR; with fixed cash flows the price must fall when the required yield rises - the defining property of fixed income.

flashcards.back: Face (par): principal repaid at maturity, typically \$1,000. Coupon: periodic interest as % of face. Maturity: the repayment date. Holder is a lender, not an owner.
$P = F(1 - d \times \text{days}/360)$: a 4.25% discount rate on 91 days and \$10,000 face gives \$9,892.57.
$P = \sum_t C/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^n$; the 2-year 4% annual-coupon bond at 5% = \$981.41, below par.
Clean: quoted price excluding accrued interest; dirty = clean + accrued (what you actually pay). Treasury quotes: 99-16 = 99 16/32 = 99.50 per \$100 face.
